summary: Defines management objects for monitoring DNS resolver functions, the client side of name lookups. It was produced by the DNS working group. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Gauges that show how a computer's name-lookup helper is doing when it asks for addresses.

subtitle: Management tools for monitoring DNS lookups on client computers.

tldr.problem: Network operators had no standard way to monitor and manage the DNS resolver software running on client machines.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1612 defines a set of management information base (MIB) objects that expose resolver configuration, statistics, caches and error conditions to SNMP-based monitoring systems.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is now Historic, replaced by newer DNS management standards, but it pioneered monitoring of resolver behavior in large networks.

today: RFC 1612 is Historic. While some resolvers may still expose these objects, the IETF community has moved toward other management frameworks for monitoring DNS. However, the architectural approach of organizing resolver state into logical groups remains relevant to DNS operations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1612 defines Management Information Base (MIB) extensions for the Domain Name System (DNS) resolver—the software that handles DNS lookups on client machines. It provides a structured set of objects that SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) managers can read and, in some cases, configure. Before this RFC, there was no standard way for network operators to monitor resolver behavior across their networks.

The MIB is organized into several logical groups: resolver configuration (which servers it knows about), performance counters (queries sent and received), detection of lame delegations (broken DNS chains), and caches (both positive and negative). This allows operators to instrument DNS behavior at scale.
sections.eli5: Just as a car's dashboard shows you how fast you are going and how much fuel you have, this RFC creates a dashboard for DNS lookups so network managers can see what is happening.

sections.title: Resolver and Server Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC divides DNS entities into two distinct roles: resolvers and name servers. A resolver is software that sends DNS queries on behalf of applications. It may be a stub resolver (which forwards all queries to a full-service server) or a full-service resolver (which can recursively resolve queries itself). A resolver may optionally maintain two types of cache: a positive cache (storing successful lookup results) and a negative cache (remembering names that do not exist). Name servers, which respond to queries, are out of scope for this MIB; they are covered by a separate RFC.

This two-role model allows the MIB to cover the wide variety of resolver implementations found in real networks, from minimal stub resolvers to complex caching servers.
sections.eli5: Some computers ask a librarian every question (stub resolver). Others learn enough to find answers themselves (full resolver). This RFC handles both kinds.

sections.title: Configuration and Performance Counters
sections.content:
The MIB groups configuration objects into a Resolver Configuration Group, which reports which resolver software is running and what type of queries it handles. The Resolver Counter Group tracks the number of queries sent and responses received, broken down by opcode (the type of query) and response code (success, failure, not-found). Additional counters report non-authoritative cached data, martian responses (answers from unexpected servers), unparseable data, and fallback events (when the resolver reverts to hardcoded default servers).

The resolver can also report uptime and reset time, allowing managers to detect restarts and assess stability.
sections.eli5: These are the scoreboard for DNS: how many questions asked, how many answers came back, how many mistakes happened.

sections.title: Caching and Lame Delegations
sections.content:
The Resolver Cache Group exposes the contents and statistics of the resolver's cache of previously resolved names. An operator can see how many records are cached, whether the cache is enabled or disabled, and even access individual cached entries. The negative cache (which stores the names and types for which no data exists) is tracked separately.

The Resolver Lame Delegation Group detects a specific class of DNS errors: lame delegations. A lame delegation occurs when a parent zone delegates a child zone to a server that does not actually answer queries for that child. The MIB maintains a table of known lame delegations, helping operators identify broken DNS infrastructure.
sections.eli5: The cache is like a notebook where the resolver writes down answers it already found so it does not have to ask again. Lame delegations are when someone points you to the wrong person to ask.

sections.title: Management and Historical Status
sections.content:
The resolver configuration includes a reset object, allowing managers to cause a resolver to reinitialize—for instance, to force it to re-read configuration files—without stopping it entirely. The Resolver Optional Counter Group provides additional statistics useful for some resolvers, such as counts of retransmissions, timeouts on internal queries, and referrals to other servers.

RFC 1612 was published in May 1994 as a Standards Track specification under SNMPv2. It became Historic because DNS operations and monitoring practices evolved. Newer work in the IETF has produced alternative monitoring approaches, and many modern DNS resolvers use different management frameworks. However, the structure and design of this MIB remain influential in network management practice.
sections.eli5: Managers can poke the resolver to make it restart and check for extra statistics when needed. Over time, better ways to monitor DNS came along, and this old way was retired.
